title: The Eighth-Grader With Seizures and Frothy Urine — Meningoencephalitis and a Kidney Under Attack

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is a 13-year-old boy in 8th standard, brought to casualty at around 10 pm in a state of post-ictal confusion. He had been apparently well 10 days earlier, then developed a low-grade, intermittent fever with chills that has persisted since. For the past four days he has had facial puffiness and swelling of his feet that come and go, along with high-colored and possibly frothy urine. For the past 3–4 days he has had headache and pain behind his eyes. For the past two days he has had bilious, non-projectile vomiting without foul smell — one episode the day before admission and 5–6 episodes on the day of admission.

On the evening of admission he had 3–4 seizures, each starting focally in his right arm and leg before generalizing, each lasting about five minutes without loss of consciousness, tongue-biting, or incontinence, followed by 20–30 minutes of post-ictal confusion. He has had no abdominal pain, loose stools, cold or cough symptoms, chest pain, palpitations, or breathlessness. He has no known history of diabetes, hypertension, asthma, epilepsy, coronary artery disease, or tuberculosis. He is a non-vegetarian with a normal appetite and regular bowel and bladder habits.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **Vitals:** temperature 98.4°F, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 89 bpm regular, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, respiratory rate 18/min, random blood glucose 196 mg/dL
- **General and systemic exam:** no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, koilonychia, lymphadenopathy, or pedal edema; heart sounds normal without murmurs; bilateral air entry with normal vesicular breath sounds; abdomen soft and non-tender without masses or organomegaly
- **Neurological exam:** higher mental functions intact, no meningeal irritation (Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs negative), cranial nerves, motor and sensory systems intact, and symmetric 2+ reflexes throughout with flexor plantar responses
- **Blood counts:** hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 16,100 with 92% neutrophils and 4% lymphocytes, RBC 3.84 million/cu.mm, platelets 2.48 lakh/cu.mm
- **Urinalysis:** reddish-yellow, hazy urine with 3+ albumin, no sugar, 2–4 pus cells/HPF, 2–3 epithelial cells/HPF, and 10–15 RBC/HPF; spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 4.1 (protein 142 mg/dL, creatinine 34 mg/dL)
- **Coagulation and renal function:** bleeding time 2 minutes, clotting time 4 minutes, PT 17 seconds, INR 1.22, APTT 35 seconds, serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL
- **Electrolytes and liver function:** sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL
- **CSF analysis:** glucose 72 mg/dL, protein 32 mg/dL, chloride 116 mg/dL; cytology showed a total count of 3 cells/cu.mm, all lymphocytes, with red cells present but no neutrophils
- **Imaging:** chest X-ray and ECG performed; MRI brain showed T2-FLAIR sulcal hyperintensities in both occipital, frontal, and parietal lobes and the right cerebellar hemisphere, with diffusion restriction in some of the right occipital and cerebellar lesions, an appearance read as suggestive of meningoencephalitis
- **Serology:** dengue IgM positive

**Working diagnosis at admission:** acute meningoencephalitis, possibly viral.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
He was started on empiric therapy for meningoencephalitis (ceftriaxone and vancomycin), IV dexamethasone, phenytoin for seizure control, and supportive medications, with strict vital sign monitoring.

Over the following days his course was tracked closely. On the first day after admission he reported improved appetite but had severe back pain at the lumbar puncture site and mild headache; his neck stiffness was noted, and he was assessed as having partially treated meningoencephalitis with associated glomerulonephritis (given the frothy, blood-tinged urine and heavy proteinuria) in the setting of dengue IgM positivity, with no adverse reaction to vancomycin. Fever, vomiting, seizures, and appetite had all begun to improve, though fever and backache persisted.

By the following day, his backache was subsiding, though low-grade fever and frothy, blood-tinged urine persisted; his appetite, seizures, and edema had resolved. He was assessed as having viral encephalitis with resolving tachycardia and fever, and his dexamethasone was continued with a plan to taper, alongside a five-day course of ceftriaxone and vancomycin.

Over the next several days his backache continued to subside and low-grade fever persisted, with his working diagnosis refined to viral encephalitis with acute glomerulonephritis. By the fourth day after admission, he had no headache, no loss of appetite, no fever, and no further seizures, and felt symptomatically much better; his vitals had normalized. The team planned a 24-hour urinary protein-creatinine ratio, repeat urinalysis, and abdominal ultrasound as advised by the nephrology team. His medications were adjusted to sodium valproate for seizure prophylaxis, along with supportive medications, and his dexamethasone was stopped at this point.
